newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya moves to curb illegal sugar imports.
newsitem.headline: Kenya moves to curb illegal sugar imports.

text.p: Kenyan authorities have announced new measures to stem illegal sugar imports and have impounded thousands of tonnes labelled for transhipment but found stored privately.

Senior officials of the Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) told Reuters that shippers of sugar in transit for other countries must now deposit with the customs department a bankers' guarantee against imports into the local market.
Finance ministry officials have in recent weeks complained about sugar making its way into the Kenyan market without any taxes being paid, making it cheaper than local produce.
Kenya Ports Authority officials have detained two ships that arrived at Mombasa with 9,600 tonnes of sugar for transhipment.
The Ar Arrabu with 6,600 tonnes from Thailand arrived on April 12, while the Trunorsk with 3,000 tonnes from Sudan arrived on April 14.
Both were being held while importers sought clearance papers that met the new regulations.
Customs officials said they had seized sugar worth 110 million shillings found stored in a private home instead of a bonded warehouse.

Customs, Kenya Revenue Authority and Kenya Sugar Authority officials said they had also seized 250,000 100-kg bags of sugar in a warehouse. They suspected the sugar was labelled as being in transit but then offloaded into Kenya.

Kenya Sugar Authority Chief Executive Francis Chahonyo last week told state KBC radio he had demanded from ports authorities details of sugar imports so far this year and taxes levied on them. He said he wanted all tax evaders severely punished.
In February, President Daniel arap Moi ordered a crackdown on illegal imports after local millers complained that they were unable to sell their sugar due to unfair competition.

In 1995, Kenya raised value added tax on imports to six from five per cent, confirmed a sugar development levy of 20 per cent, raised a blanket sugar levy to 25 from 15 percent and launched a variable dumping duty of $105.83 per tonne.

But in the first quarter of this year the government suspended taxes on essential commodities to encourage imports for drought relief. Government officials said the all sugar taxes had since been restored.
KPA officials said Kenya had imported 105,270 tonnes of sugar in the first quarter of the year. They did not provide comparative figures for last year.
Kenya's production is forecast at around 420,000 tonnes in 1997 against consumption of 560,000 tonnes.

The ports authority figures show most sugar was imported from Brazil, Thailand, Romania, India, Britain, Belgium and Paraguay. Thailand was the dominant player in the market, with 39,849 tonnes. Brazil, from where 101,236 tonnes was sourced last year, provided only 9,012 tonnes in the first quarter.
